beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Hola — this is Liam, in for Divyank. A model can state a fabricated citation and a true one in exactly the same confident prose — and a real lawyer actually got fined for trusting one. This chapter is the discipline against that: how a single claim earns the right to stay in the book, by being checked, recorded, and signed.

beats.act: Act I — A Fact Is a Record, Not a Recollection
beats.narration_text: Models state fabricated facts — invented statistics, citations to cases that never existed — in exactly the same confident prose they use for true ones. Fluency was never proof.

beats.act: Act I — A Fact Is a Record, Not a Recollection
beats.narration_text: The defense isn't a better model. It's a discipline: never let one fluent answer stand in for verification. This book gives that discipline a home — facts dot j-s-o-n.

beats.act: Act II — Three Rules, Straight From the Constitution
beats.narration_text: Before any fresh search, the rule is to look at what's already been checked. A recorded fact beats a fresh guess — the cheapest verification is the one somebody already did.

beats.act: Act II — Three Rules, Straight From the Constitution

beats.act: Act II — Three Rules, Straight From the Constitution
beats.narration_text: Rule two: new facts enter unverified. Every new entry starts verified-false — source-attested, not yet authoritative — and stays that way until a human actually signs it.

beats.act: Act II — Three Rules, Straight From the Constitution
beats.narration_text: A verified fact can grow or it can break. New evidence gets appended, and the signature stays intact. Edit the entry itself instead, and the audit trail is gone.

beats.act: Act II — Three Rules, Straight From the Constitution
beats.narration_text: Consensus — agreement, conflict, or unverified — is computed from the evidence list. Nobody types it in by hand. You don't declare consensus. The evidence does.

beats.act: Act II — Three Rules, Straight From the Constitution
beats.narration_text: That's exactly why the system is auditable: you can always see who attested what, when they attested it, and whether the sources actually agree.

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A fact is a record, not a recollection — models state fabricated claims with the same fluent confidence as true ones, which is exactly why facts dot j-s-o-n exists. Three rules do the real work: check facts dot j-s-o-n before searching, every new fact starts verified-false, and a verified fact is never overwritten, only appended to. The exercise is trace, add, sign, and refuse: tracing a claim to its source, recording a new one as unverified, then signing what you'll vouch for and refusing, with a reason, what you won't. And the chapter's own failure table covers the rest: an unsourced claim, a fact signed without being sure, two disagreeing sources, and an edited signature — each one has a specific, honest fix.
